claim: Mouse CA1 pyramidal neurons express apamin-sensitive SK2-containing channels in the post-synaptic membrane.
source: Mouse CA1 pyramidal neurons express apamin-sensitive SK2-containing channels in the post-synaptic membrane, positioned close to NMDA-type (N-methyl-D-aspartate) glutamate receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing apamin-sensitive responses in CA1 pyramidal neurons.

claim: Synaptic SK2-containing channels are positioned close to NMDA-type glutamate receptors.
source: Mouse CA1 pyramidal neurons express apamin-sensitive SK2-containing channels in the post-synaptic membrane, positioned close to NMDA-type (N-methyl-D-aspartate) glutamate receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and referenced in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: Synaptic SK2-containing channels are activated by synaptically evoked NMDAR-dependent Ca2+ influx.
source: Activated by synaptically evoked NMDAR-dependent Ca2+ influx, the synaptic SK2-containing channels modulate excitatory post-synaptic responses and the induction of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work (Ngo-Anh et al., 2005).

claim: Synaptic SK2-containing channels modulate excitatory post-synaptic responses.
source: Activated by synaptically evoked NMDAR-dependent Ca2+ influx, the synaptic SK2-containing channels modulate excitatory post-synaptic responses and the induction of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by experimental data showing apamin effects on EPSPs.

claim: Synaptic SK2-containing channels modulate the induction of synaptic plasticity.
source: Activated by synaptically evoked NMDAR-dependent Ca2+ influx, the synaptic SK2-containing channels modulate excitatory post-synaptic responses and the induction of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by LTP experiments showing reduced LTP with MPP2 knockdown.

claim: Activity- and protein kinase A-dependent trafficking of SK2-containing channels contributes to expression of long-term potentiation.
source: In addition, their activity- and protein kinase A-dependent trafficking contributes to expression of long-term potentiation (LTP).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work (Lin et al., 2008).

claim: MPP2 is a member of the membrane-associated guanylate kinase (MAGUK) family.
source: We have identified a novel synaptic scaffold, MPP2 (membrane palmitoylated protein 2; p55), a member of the membrane-associated guanylate kinase (MAGUK) family that interacts with SK2-containing channels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis showing MPP2 contains characteristic MAGUK domains.

claim: MPP2 interacts with SK2-containing channels.
source: We have identified a novel synaptic scaffold, MPP2 (membrane palmitoylated protein 2; p55), a member of the membrane-associated guanylate kinase (MAGUK) family that interacts with SK2-containing channels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation and co-immunopurification experiments.

claim: MPP2 and SK2 co-immunopurified from mouse brain.
source: MPP2 and SK2 co-immunopurified from mouse brain, and co-immunoprecipitated when they were co-expressed in HEK293 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 1C with mass spectrometry data.

claim: MPP2 and SK2 co-immunoprecipitated when co-expressed in HEK293 cells.
source: MPP2 and SK2 co-immunopurified from mouse brain, and co-immunoprecipitated when they were co-expressed in HEK293 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MPP2 is highly expressed in the post-synaptic density of dendritic spines on CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: MPP2 is highly expressed in the post-synaptic density of dendritic spines on CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by electron microscopy in Figure 3.

claim: Knocking down MPP2 expression selectively abolished the SK2-containing channel contribution to synaptic responses.
source: Knocking down MPP2 expression selectively abolished the SK2-containing channel contribution to synaptic responses and decreased LTP.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by electrophysiology experiments showing loss of apamin sensitivity in Figure 4.

claim: Knocking down MPP2 expression decreased LTP.
source: Knocking down MPP2 expression selectively abolished the SK2-containing channel contribution to synaptic responses and decreased LTP.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by LTP experiments in Figure 8.

claim: MPP2 is required for proper synaptic localization and function of SK2-containing channels.
source: Thus, MPP2 is a novel synaptic scaffold that is required for proper synaptic localization and function of SK2-containing channels.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by the combined data from knockdown experiments.

claim: At Schaffer collateral to CA1 synapses, excitatory neurotransmission is largely mediated by ionotropic AMPA-type and NMDA-type glutamate receptors.
source: At most excitatory synapses in the central nervous system, such as the Schaffer collateral to CA1 synapses in the stratum radiatum of the hippocampus, excitatory neurotransmission is largely mediated by ionotropic AMPA-type (α-Amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid) and NMDA-type glutamate receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Synaptically evoked Ca2+ influx into dendritic spines activates apamin-sensitive SK2-containing channels.
source: For example, synaptically evoked Ca2+ influx into dendritic spines activates apamin-sensitive SK2-containing channels (small conductance Ca2+-activated K+ channels type 2; KCNN2), and their outward K+ conductance shunts the AMPAR-mediated depolarization, effectively reducing the EPSP (Ngo-Anh et al., 2005; Faber et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: The outward K+ conductance of SK2-containing channels shunts the AMPAR-mediated depolarization, effectively reducing the EPSP.
source: For example, synaptically evoked Ca2+ influx into dendritic spines activates apamin-sensitive SK2-containing channels (small conductance Ca2+-activated K+ channels type 2; KCNN2), and their outward K+ conductance shunts the AMPAR-mediated depolarization, effectively reducing the EPSP (Ngo-Anh et al., 2005; Faber et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: Kv4.2-containing channels are expressed in spines, close to, but not in the PSD.
source: Kv4.2-containing channels are expressed in spines, close to, but not in the PSD (Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: Synaptic activity evokes Ca2+ influx through R-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in spines that boosts nearby Kv4.2-containing A-type K+ channels to further decrease the AMPA-mediated depolarization.
source: Synaptic activity evokes Ca2+ influx through R-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in spines that boosts nearby Kv4.2-containing A-type K+ channels to further decrease the AMPA-mediated depolarization (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: Ca2+-activated Cl- channels are expressed in the spines and provide inhibitory contributions.
source: In addition, Ca2+-activated Cl- channels are expressed in the spines and provide further inhibitory contributions (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: The sum of repolarizing conductances may reduce the depolarizing AMPA-NMDA component by more than 50%.
source: Indeed, the sum of these repolarizing conductances may reduce the depolarizing AMPA-NMDA component by more than 50%.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from the combined effects of multiple conductances.

claim: The Ca2+ sensitivity of SK2 channels is regulated in an activity-dependent manner by co-assembled protein kinase CK2 and protein phosphatase 2A.
source: For example, the Ca2+ sensitivity of SK2 channels is regulated in an activity-dependent manner by co-assembled protein kinase CK2 and protein phosphatase 2A (Bildl et al., 2004; Allen et al., 2007) that are engaged by cholinergic signaling (Giessel and Sabatini, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: CK2 and protein phosphatase 2A associated with SK2 channels are engaged by cholinergic signaling.
source: For example, the Ca2+ sensitivity of SK2 channels is regulated in an activity-dependent manner by co-assembled protein kinase CK2 and protein phosphatase 2A (Bildl et al., 2004; Allen et al., 2007) that are engaged by cholinergic signaling (Giessel and Sabatini, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: Synaptic SK2-containing channels undergo protein kinase A (PKA)-dependent endocytosis upon the induction of LTP by theta burst pairing.
source: Synaptic SK2-containing channels undergo protein kinase A (PKA)-dependent endocytosis upon the induction of LTP by theta burst pairing.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work (Lin et al., 2008).

claim: The endocytosis of synaptic SK2-containing channels acts together with the PKA-dependent exocytosis of additional GluA1-containing AMPARs to mediate the expression of LTP.
source: The endocytosis of synaptic SK2-containing channels acts together with the PKA-dependent exocytosis of additional GluA1-containing AMPARs to mediate the expression of LTP (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: After the initial expression of LTP and loss of the SK2-containing channel contribution, homeostatic mechanisms act to re-establish the synaptic SK balance.
source: Moreover, after the initial expression of LTP and loss of the SK2-containing channel contribution, homeostatic mechanisms act to re-establish the synaptic SK balance (Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: Kv4.2-containing channels expressed in spines undergo PKA-dependent endocytosis after the induction of LTP.
source: Similarly, Kv4.2-containing channels expressed in spines undergo PKA-dependent endocytosis after the induction of LTP (Kim et al., 2007; Hammond et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: MAGUKs bind to synaptic receptors, channels, and signaling molecules to anchor them into their proper locations within the post-synaptic membrane.
source: These modular, usually multivalent scaffolds bind to synaptic receptors, channels, and signaling molecules to anchor them into their proper locations within the post-synaptic membrane (Oliva et al., 2012), creating a spatially and temporally restricted signaling domain (Hammond et al., 2008; Colledge et al., 2000; Dell'Acqua et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: PSD-95 binds to NMDARs within the post-synaptic density of excitatory synapses.
source: Thus, within the post-synaptic density of excitatory synapses PSD-95 binds to NMDARs (Cousins and Stephenson, 2012), while SAP97 binds to AMPARs (Howard et al., 2010; Leonard et al., 1998), and Shank and Homer may serve as modular organizers of the lattice of synaptic MAGUKs (Sheng and Kim, 2000; Hayashi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: SAP97 binds to AMPARs within the post-synaptic density of excitatory synapses.
source: Thus, within the post-synaptic density of excitatory synapses PSD-95 binds to NMDARs (Cousins and Stephenson, 2012), while SAP97 binds to AMPARs (Howard et al., 2010; Leonard et al., 1998), and Shank and Homer may serve as modular organizers of the lattice of synaptic MAGUKs (Sheng and Kim, 2000; Hayashi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: Shank and Homer may serve as modular organizers of the lattice of synaptic MAGUKs.
source: Thus, within the post-synaptic density of excitatory synapses PSD-95 binds to NMDARs (Cousins and Stephenson, 2012), while SAP97 binds to AMPARs (Howard et al., 2010; Leonard et al., 1998), and Shank and Homer may serve as modular organizers of the lattice of synaptic MAGUKs (Sheng and Kim, 2000; Hayashi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: There are two major isoforms of SK2 that are expressed in CA1 pyramidal neurons: SK2-L (long) and SK2-S (short).
source: There are two major isoforms of SK2 that are expressed in CA1 pyramidal neurons; SK2-L (long) has an extended intracellular N-terminal domain compared to SK2-S (short) and the two isoforms co-assemble into heteromeric channels (Strassmaier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: SK2-L has an extended intracellular N-terminal domain compared to SK2-S.
source: There are two major isoforms of SK2 that are expressed in CA1 pyramidal neurons; SK2-L (long) has an extended intracellular N-terminal domain compared to SK2-S (short) and the two isoforms co-assemble into heteromeric channels (Strassmaier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: SK2-L and SK2-S co-assemble into heteromeric channels.
source: There are two major isoforms of SK2 that are expressed in CA1 pyramidal neurons; SK2-L (long) has an extended intracellular N-terminal domain compared to SK2-S (short) and the two isoforms co-assemble into heteromeric channels (Strassmaier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: In mice that selectively lack SK2-L expression, the SK2-S channels are expressed in the plasma membrane of dendrites and dendritic spines, yet fail to become incorporated into the post-synaptic membrane.
source: In mice that selectively lack SK2-L expression, the SK2-S channels are expressed in the plasma membrane of dendrites and dendritic spines, yet fail to become incorporated into the post-synaptic membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work (Allen et al., 2011).

claim: In mice lacking SK2-L expression, the SK2-containing channel contributions to EPSPs and plasticity are absent.
source: Consequently, the SK2-containing channel contributions to EPSPs and plasticity are absent, and this loss of synaptic SK2-containing channel function enhances hippocampus-dependent learning tasks (Allen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of synaptic SK2-containing channel function enhances hippocampus-dependent learning tasks.
source: Consequently, the SK2-containing channel contributions to EPSPs and plasticity are absent, and this loss of synaptic SK2-containing channel function enhances hippocampus-dependent learning tasks (Allen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: Both anti-MPP2 antibodies robustly purified MPP2 and co-purified SK2 as well as SK3.
source: The results demonstrated that both antibodies robustly purified MPP2 and co-purified SK2 as well as SK3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C with mass spectrometry data.

claim: Proteomic analyses identified DLG1 (SAP97) and Lin-homologs 7A and 7C as proteins co-assembling with MPP2 in rodent brain.
source: In addition, these experiments identified DLG1 (SAP97) and Lin-homologs 7A and 7C as proteins co-assembling with MPP2 in rodent brain (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C with mass spectrometry data.

claim: MPP2 is a 552 amino acid protein.
source: MPP2, a member of the p55 Stardust family of MAGUK proteins, is predicted to be a 552 amino acid protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence analysis.

claim: MPP2 contains two predicted L27 domains, followed by a single predicted PDZ domain, and then the SH3-HOOK-GK domains.
source: There are two predicted L27 domains, followed by a single predicted PDZ domain, and then the SH3-HOOK-GK domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural prediction.

claim: C8-MPP2 but not PSD-95 was specifically co-precipitated with SK2 when co-expressed in HEK293 cells.
source: The results demonstrated that C8-MPP2 but not PSD-95 was specifically co-precipitated with SK2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: C8-SAP97 co-immunoprecipitated with GluA1 but not with SK2-S when co-expressed in HEK293 cells.
source: Western blotting with anti-C8 antibody revealed that C8-SAP97 only co-immunoprecipitated when co-expressed with GluA1, despite equivalent levels of input and immunoprecipitated proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SH3-HOOK-GK domain of MPP2 specifically pulled down the N-terminal domain of SK2-L.
source: Probing with an anti-His antibody showed that the SH3-HOOK-GK domain from MPP2, but not from SAP97 or CaCNB4, specifically pulled down the N-terminal domain of SK2-L.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MPP2 interacts with the unique N-terminal domain of SK2-L that is required for synaptic localization.
source: Taken together these results suggest that MPP2 interacts with the unique N-terminal domain of SK2-L that is required for synaptic localization (Allen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the GST pull-down experiments, with citation to previous work.

claim: MPP2 was expressed throughout the hippocampus, and in area CA1, MPP2 was predominantly expressed in the dendritic arbors.
source: At the light level, MPP2 was expressed throughout the hippocampus, and in area CA1, MPP2 was predominantly expressed in the dendritic arbors (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Using pre-embedding techniques, immunoparticles for MPP2 prominently labeled dendritic spines and dendritic shafts both along the plasma membrane and at intracellular sites.
source: Using pre-embedding techniques, sections from three animals revealed immunoparticles for MPP2 prominently labeled dendritic spines and dendritic shafts both along the plasma membrane and at intracellular sites.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on electron microscopy data.

claim: Most immunoparticles for MPP2 were found in spines (84%; 436 particles) versus in dendrites (16%; 82 immunoparticles).
source: Post-synaptically, most immunoparticles for MPP2 were found in spines (84%; 436 particles) versus in dendrites (16%; 82 immunoparticles), with most immunoparticles in either compartment localized to the plasma membrane (84%; 365 immunoparticles in spines and 65%; 54 immunoparticles in dendrites).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on quantitative electron microscopy data.

claim: Using post-embedding techniques, immunoparticles for MPP2 prominently labeled the post-synaptic densities of dendritic spines.
source: Next, post-embedding techniques were applied to determine if MPP2 is expressed in the post-synaptic density. Sections from three animals revealed that immunoparticles for MPP2 prominently labeled the post-synaptic densities of dendritic spines, as well as being detected in dendritic shafts (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Immunoparticles for MPP2 were not detected in stratum pyramidale, and were also absent pre-synaptically.
source: Immunoparticles for MPP2 were not detected in stratum pyramidale, and were also absent pre-synaptically.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on electron microscopy data.

claim: For control cells, apamin increased EPSPs to 144.4 ± 4.3% of baseline (n = 15; p<0.0001).
source: For control cells, apamin increased EPSPs to 144.4 ± 4.3% of baseline (n = 15; p<0.0001), consistent with previous studies (Ngo-Anh et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2008; Giessel and Sabatini, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on electrophysiology data.

claim: In MPP2 shRNA-transfected CA1 pyramidal neurons, apamin did not significantly affect EPSPs (94.6 ± 3.3%; n = 14).
source: In contrast, apamin did not significantly affect EPSPs from transfected CA1 pyramidal neurons (94.6 ± 3.3%; n = 14) (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: In spines on neurons expressing GFP (MPP2 shRNA), immunoparticles for MPP2 were reduced by 81% compared to spines on non-transfected control neurons.
source: In spines on neurons expressing GFP, immunoparticles for MPP2 were reduced by 81% compared to spines on non-transfected control neurons (GFP-negative: 417 particles in 60 spines; GFP-positive: 101 particles in 60 spines; p<0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on quantitative electron microscopy data.

claim: In dendritic shafts of MPP2 shRNA-transfected neurons, immunoparticles for MPP2 were reduced by 78%.
source: A similar reduction (78%) was seen in dendritic shafts (GFP-negative: 155 particles in 25 dendrites; GFP-positive: 44 particles in 25 dendrites; p<0.001) (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: In doubly transfected neurons (shRNA plus shRNA-immune MPP2), apamin increased EPSPs similar to control, non-transfected neurons (148.2 ± 4.2%; n = 13; p<0.0001, compared to shRNA knock-down).
source: In doubly transfected neurons, apamin increased EPSPs similar to control, non-transfected neurons (148.2 ± 4.2%; n = 13; p<0.0001, compared to shRNA knock-down) (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: MPP2 knock-down did not significantly affect somatic activation of SK2-containing channels (ctrl: 41.9 ± 8.3 pA, n = 13; transfected: 53.7 ± 10.5, n = 7; P = 0.44).
source: The apamin-sensitive component of the tail current (Figure 7A inset) effectively measures the SK2-containing channel component activated by somatic depolarization and showed that MPP2 knock-down did not significantly affect somatic activation of SK2-containing channels (ctrl: 41.9 ± 8.3 pA, n = 13; transfected: 53.7 ± 10.5, n = 7; P = 0.44) (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Knocking down MPP2 expression disrupts the synaptic SK2-containing channel component but does not affect the channels in the dendrites that are activated by somatic voltage pulses.
source: These results show that knocking down MPP2 expression disrupts the synaptic SK2-containing channel component but does not affect the channels in the dendrites that are activated by somatic voltage pulses.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the voltage-clamp experiments.

claim: In non-transfected CA1 pyramidal neurons, theta burst pairing induced LTP of 407.9 ± 46.3% (n = 8).
source: In non-transfected CA1 pyramidal neurons, this induced LTP of 407.9 ± 46.3% (n = 8), while in transfected, MPP2 knock down neurons, LTP was significantly reduced (243.0 ± 14.8%; n = 13; p<0.001) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: In transfected, MPP2 knock down neurons, LTP was significantly reduced (243.0 ± 14.8%; n = 13; p<0.001).
source: In non-transfected CA1 pyramidal neurons, this induced LTP of 407.9 ± 46.3% (n = 8), while in transfected, MPP2 knock down neurons, LTP was significantly reduced (243.0 ± 14.8%; n = 13; p<0.001) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: In CA1 pyramidal neurons expressing shRNAs directed against Mpp2 mRNA, apamin has no effect on synaptically evoked EPSPs.
source: Synaptically evoked EPSPs in CA1 pyramidal neurons are increased by the SK channel blocker, apamin, but in CA1 pyramidal neurons expressing shRNAs directed against Mpp2 mRNA apamin has no effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: MPP2 knockdown selectively affects synaptic SK2-containing channel function, as the SK2-containing channels expressed in the dendrites that are activated by somatic voltage steps are not altered.
source: MPP2 knockdown selectively affects synaptic SK2-containing channel function, as the SK2-containing channels expressed in the dendrites that are activated by somatic voltage steps are not altered.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: MPP2 knock-down reduces the expression of TBP-induced LTP by ~30%.
source: Consistent with the effects of MPP2 on synaptic SK2-containing channels, MPP2 knock-down reduces the expression of TBP-induced LTP by ~30%.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the LTP data.

claim: The component of LTP attributed to SK2 endocytosis in untransfected CA1 pyramidal neurons is ~17%.
source: This is slightly more than the component of LTP attributed to SK2 endocytosis in untransfected CA1 pyramidal neurons, ~17% (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to previous work.

claim: Synaptic SK2-containing channels are heteromeric assemblies that contain two isoforms of SK2, SK2-S and SK2-L.
source: Previous results showed that synaptic SK2-containing channels are heteromeric assemblies that contain two isoforms of SK2, SK2-S and SK2-L.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to previous work.

claim: SK2-L has an additional 207 amino acids in the intracellular N-terminal domain compared to SK2-S.
source: Compared to SK2-S, SK2-L has an additional 207 amino acids in the intracellular N-terminal domain and SK2-S is otherwise entirely contained in SK2-L (Strassmaier et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to previous work.

claim: In a transgenic mouse selectively lacking SK2-L, the SK2-S channels are expressed in the dendrites and even in the plasma membrane of dendritic spines, but they are specifically excluded from the PSD.
source: In a transgenic mouse selectively lacking SK2-L, the SK2-S channels are expressed in the dendrites and even in the plasma membrane of dendritic spines, but they are specifically excluded from the PSD, and apamin fails to boost synaptically evoked EPSPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to previous work (Allen et al., 2011).

claim: Re-expressing SK2-L reinstates synaptic function as measured by apamin sensitivity of EPSPs.
source: Re-expressing SK2-L reinstates synaptic function as measured by apamin sensitivity of EPSPs (Allen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to previous work.

claim: The unique N-terminal domain of SK2-L is implicated in directing SK2-containing channel synaptic localization and function.
source: These results implicated the unique N-terminal domain of SK2-L in directing SK2-containing channel synaptic localization and function, and suggested that the N-terminal domain of SK2-L might interact with a partner protein to engender PSD localization.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from previous work.

claim: MPP2 binds to the unique N-terminal domain of SK2-L and knocking down MPP2 expression phenocopied the effect of SK2-L deletion on synaptic responses.
source: Indeed, MPP2 binds to the unique N-terminal domain and knocking down MPP2 expression phenocopied the effect of SK2-L deletion on synaptic responses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: MPP2 serves to stabilize SK2-containing channels in the PSD.
source: Our results suggest that MPP2 similarly serves to stabilize SK2-containing channels in the PSD.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: MPP2 is a member of the p55 Stardust subfamily of MAGUK scaffold proteins.
source: MPP2 is a member of the p55 Stardust subfamily of MAGUK scaffold proteins, named after the founding member MPP1, the major palmitoylated protein in erythrocytes (Alloisio et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to previous work.

claim: MPP2 consists of two L27 domains that may mediate homo- or heterophilic interactions, a single PDZ domain followed by SH3-HOOK-GK domains.
source: Similar to other MAGUK scaffold proteins, MPP2 is modular, consisting of two L27 domains that may mediate homo- or heterophilic interactions, a single PDZ domain followed by SH3-HOOK-GK domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on structural analysis.

claim: Biochemical studies showed that MPP2 is enriched in the PSD fractions of rat brain.
source: Biochemical studies showed that MPP2 is enriched in the PSD fractions of rat brain, and pull-down assays to test for interactions suggested MPP2 may interact with itself as well as a number of other synaptic proteins, among them are PSD-95, SAP97, GKAP, CASK, GRIP, neuroligin, and CaMKII.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to previous work (Jing-Ping et al., 2005).

claim: The SH3-HOOK-GK domain of MPP2 was implicated in mediating interactions with other synaptic proteins.
source: The SH3-HOOK-GK domain of MPP2 was implicated in mediating these interactions (Jing-Ping et al., 2005), similar to the interaction between MPP2 and the N-terminal domain of SK2-L.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to previous work.

claim: SK2 and SK3 can form heteromeric channels in brain.
source: SK2 and SK3 can form heteromeric channels in brain (Strassmaier et al., 2005), and SK3 is expressed in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Ballesteros-Merino et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous work.

claim: SK3 is expressed in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: SK2 and SK3 can form heteromeric channels in brain (Strassmaier et al., 2005), and SK3 is expressed in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Ballesteros-Merino et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to previous work.

claim: There is only one SK3 N-terminal isoform and it is similar to the extended N-terminal domain of SK2-L, harboring several islands of homology that might mediate interactions with MPP2.
source: Different from SK2 that has two N-terminal isoforms, there is only one SK3 N-terminal isoform and it is similar to the extended N-terminal domain of SK2-L, harboring several islands of homology that might mediate interactions with MPP2.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on sequence analysis.

claim: In epithelial cells, MPP7 dimerizes with Lin7 proteins, an interaction mediated by the C-terminal L27 domain.
source: In epithelial cells, MPP7, a closely related member of the p55 Stardust family, dimerizes with Lin7 proteins, an interaction mediated by the C-terminal L27 domain, and the dimeric complex then associates with DLG1 via the N-terminal L27 domain that is insufficient to mediate DLG1 interactions in the absence of bound Lin7 (Bohl et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to previous work.

claim: The MPP7-Lin7 dimeric complex associates with DLG1 via the N-terminal L27 domain.
source: In epithelial cells, MPP7, a closely related member of the p55 Stardust family, dimerizes with Lin7 proteins, an interaction mediated by the C-terminal L27 domain, and the dimeric complex then associates with DLG1 via the N-terminal L27 domain that is insufficient to mediate DLG1 interactions in the absence of bound Lin7 (Bohl et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to previous work.

claim: DLG1 binds the C-terminal PDZ ligand on the GluA1 subunit of AMPA receptors.
source: DLG1 also binds the C-terminal PDZ ligand on the GluA1 subunit of AMPA receptors (Leonard et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to previous work.

claim: Upon the induction of LTP at Schaffer collateral to CA1 synapses, additional GluA1-containing AMPA receptors undergo exocytosis at a perisynaptic site followed by translocation into the post-synaptic membrane, increasing the AMPA component of EPSPs.
